title: AI Learning App
description: UI/UX overhaul and design system for an AI-powered learning platform at Carnegie Mellon.

caseStudy.blurb: A six-month UI/UX overhaul of the Search Ad Strategy Lab, an AI-powered simulation Carnegie Mellon's Tepper School of Business uses to teach digital advertising. I led the redesign end to end and rebuilt it on a design system — semantic color, one type family, and components specified across every state — then applied that system to the five modules a student works through.
caseStudy.overview:
Tepper teaches digital advertising with a simulation. A student interviews an AI research agent to learn a client's market and goals, tests keyword ideas against estimated bid ranges and competition, assembles keywords, bids, and ad copy into a campaign, then reads the performance data back and recommends what to change. Five modules, start to finish.

The teaching material was strong. The interface it ran on had grown feature by feature over several years and had stopped keeping up. I came on as the sole designer for six months to redesign it and hand the result to the engineering team as a working system rather than a set of screens.
caseStudy.team: Client: Carnegie Mellon University, Tepper School of Business
objectives: Redesign all five student modules — research, keyword testing, campaign submission, performance detail, and summary — so the interface teaches the concept instead of competing with it.
Replace accumulated one-off styling with a documented token and component system the engineering team can build against.
Specify every component state, including the empty and failure cases the original screens left undefined.
Produce developer-ready specifications for a TypeScript/React frontend, not just static mockups.
caseStudy.challenge:
The platform had been extended one feature at a time, and it showed. Buttons that did the same thing looked different on different pages. Type sizes had drifted into a range wide enough that nothing read as deliberate. Dense numerical views — bid tables, campaign performance — gave inputs, results, and labels the same visual weight, so students had to work out what they were looking at before they could work out what it meant.

That last part is the real problem in an educational product. Every second a student spends decoding the interface is a second not spent learning how an ad auction behaves. The interface was adding difficulty in a place where the subject already supplies plenty.

The constraint was that this had to land as something a small engineering team could actually implement. A redesign that looked good in Figma and took a year to build would not have been useful to anyone.
caseStudy.approach:
I started by mapping what already existed rather than by drawing screens — every page, every component variant, every color and type value in use. Seeing the real inventory made the priority obvious: redundancy in the component set was the root cause, and the visual inconsistency was a symptom of it.

So the system came first. One type family, Open Sans, across six roles from a 32px title down to a 14px caption. A semantic palette built around a single action blue, with separate positive, warning, and danger values — and CMU's carmine held back for brand alone. That last decision mattered more than it looks: a university red and an error red in the same interface would have made students read institutional identity as something going wrong.

Components came next, on top of the tokens: four button variants across default, hover, and disabled, on 40px targets; text, search, checkbox, and radio controls all bound to those same tokens. Building the foundation first turned the screen redesigns into composition work instead of a series of one-off decisions, and it meant engineering received something with a structure they already recognised.

Only then did I rework the flows. Campaign submission was restructured so setup reads as a sequence — headline, audience, bid — rather than one dense form. Keyword research was reorganised around the comparison a student is actually making. The performance views were rebuilt to lead with the result and put supporting detail second.

userExperience.description: The users here are students under time pressure, working through a module, usually with nobody beside them to ask. That framing settled most of the interface questions. Where a general-purpose product might reasonably favour density and speed for repeat users, this one had to favour legibility for someone meeting the screen for the first and possibly only time. The course rail carries that: progress, what each module asks of you, and how long it should take, visible without leaving the screen you are on.
insights: In a teaching tool, interface friction and subject difficulty are indistinguishable to the learner. A confused student rarely stops to work out which one is confusing them — they just conclude the material is hard.
Consistency did more work than any individual screen improvement. Once a button meant one thing everywhere, the flows needed noticeably less explanation around them.

Specifying the empty, zero-result, and failure states up front surfaced product questions the original screens had quietly left unanswered — what a student sees before entering a first keyword, and what happens when the simulation service does not respond.
Designing for handoff changed the design itself. Knowing every variant had to map to a prop pushed me to reduce the component set rather than expand it.

caseStudy.solution:
The delivered work was a Figma design system plus the five module flows built from it. The system covers the token foundation, a component library with every state specified, and the page-level patterns — the course rail that carries progress across modules, the module content layouts, the data views, and the completion summary that closes a lab and points at what to take next.

The handoff was structured for a TypeScript/React codebase: components named and organised the way they would be implemented, states enumerated rather than implied, and specifications detailed enough to build from without a follow-up conversation for every screen.
